episode_summary: Corey Petty and Colin Couchet interview Blockstream Director of Research Andrew Poelstra about why ECDSA is not a strong signature, the history of transaction malleability and SegWit, the Schnorr signature patent story, and Taproot with Pay-to-Contract. They also cover Mimblewimble, adaptor signatures, and criticism of Ethereum's design and node storage costs.

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said transaction malleability was a really big deal before SegWit.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: This used to be a really big deal before Segwit.

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra explained third-party malleability: an attacker could alter a transaction's signature, changing its transaction ID while keeping it valid.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: somebody is able to tweak your signature somehow, or like add padding to your signature or do something

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra explained first-party malleability: each co-signer's signature changed a multisig transaction's TXID.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: every time somebody adds their own signature to the transaction, that causes the TXID to change

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra described SegWit as moving witness data, including signatures, out of the part of the transaction that feeds the transaction ID.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: the witness data, which includes signatures like this, is simply moved out of the part of the transaction that goes into the TXID

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Satoshi needed a strong signature scheme, not plain ECDSA, so that transaction IDs could not be malleated.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: what Satoshi needed to use was something called a strong signature

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra explained that an ECDSA signature can be tweaked by negating its S value, because verification checks only the x-coordinate of the final point.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: in the ECDSA signature verification equation, the only thing that gets checked is the x-coordinate of the final point

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra explained that in Schnorr the nonce goes into the hash, so the signer's nonce is fixed before the message hash is chosen.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: in Schnorr, the nonce goes into the hash

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said ECDSA's nonce handling was a patent-evasion trick against the 1991 Schnorr signature patent held by Klaus Schnorr.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: the reason this is done is basically to evade a patent that Schnorr put, that Klaus Schnorr put on the Schnorr signature algorithm in 1991

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said the Schnorr patent expired in 2008, and Ed25519 in 2011 was the first use of Schnorr-style signatures he knew of after that.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: the Schnorr just didn't get used until the patent expired in 2008

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said the Schnorr patent holder made no money from it, because NIST defined ECDSA to evade the patent.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: he didn't make a dime because NIST defined the ECDSA algorithm to evade this patent

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said SHA-2 is treated as uniformly random because the most efficient known SHA-2 proof of work is just hashing over and over.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: the most efficient way to do SHA-2 proof of work that anyone found is to just hash over and over and over

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra described Taproot as a proposal that makes a Bitcoin output's witness program just a public key, spent with a Schnorr signature.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: rather than having the program be a hash of a bunch of Bitcoin script opcodes describing a program, the program will just be a public key

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Blockstream Green wallet coins were typically controlled by a 2-of-2 output, with Blockstream co-signing.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: if you use the Blockstream green wallet, I believe all the coins are controlled by a two of two output, so you need to sign and Blockstream needs to sign

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Blockstream's Liquid sidechain is federated, with 11 of 15 participants needing to sign to move coins back.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: The way that I'm aware of it being used is in Blockstream's Liquid, which is a side chain

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra explained pay to contract as tweaking an elliptic curve public key with a hash so it commits to hidden extra data.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: where you take an elliptic curve point and you add to that point another point, which is a hash of the original point and then also some extra data

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said that with Taproot an observer sees one key and one signature, and cannot tell how many signers are involved or what contract sits inside.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: it's indistinguishable how many signers are involved. It's indistinguishable what kind of threshold or weird policy of signers involved.

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Taproot is ultimately rolling your own crypto, but that new cryptography has to be reviewed by the wider community.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: ultimately, this is rolling your own crypto. But ultimately, somebody has to roll new crypto

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Confidential Transactions, developed by Greg Maxwell in 2015, replace transaction amounts with hiding, binding commitments.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: Confidential transactions was a scheme for replacing all of the inputs and outputs amounts in transactions with these hiding binding commitments

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Mimblewimble transactions are authorized by a Schnorr signature over a kernel that is both a commitment to zero and a joint public key of all participants.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: It's both a commitment to zero, and it's also a public key belonging jointly to all of the participants in the transaction

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Mimblewimble could not support hash-preimage atomic swaps or Lightning, because deleting transaction data means the chain cannot enforce them.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: You can't do this in Mimblewimble because you're deleting all of the transaction data.

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said he found a way to put hash preimages into Mimblewimble using an adaptive signature, a two-party Schnorr scheme.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: I found a way through something called an adaptive signature

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said Ethereum was a fractal of bad design choices, with a smart-contract language designed to be undecidable.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: my feeling on Ethereum more generally is that it is just a fractal of bad design choices

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said a full Ethereum node needed roughly a terabyte of storage, while a Bitcoin node was about 250 to 300 gigabytes.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: In Bitcoin, that's probably 250, almost 300 gigabytes

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said the EVM's per-contract data stores make Ethereum expensive to verify, with a full equivalent of a transaction index about a terabyte.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: If you maintain like a full equivalent to TX index on Ethereum, it's like a terabyte or something

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said the Snarks for Sea paper in October 2013 was the first hint that compact zero-knowledge proofs might be practical.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: This was the first paper that hinted that maybe these Snarks, these compact zero-knowledge proofs might be practical

cards.claim: In July 2019 Andrew Poelstra said IOTA's signatures are insecure, because an adversary who sees more than one signature learns parts of the secret key.
cards.speaker: Andrew Poelstra
cards.quote: they learn parts of the secret key, and then they can produce forged signatures using those parts of the secret key

title: Blockstream - Andrew Poelstra
